question: Consider the scenario below and answer the following questions:
sourceAnswer:
The product team has a great new feature they want to add to your Ruby on Rails application: they want every model in the system to be able to retain special user notes. You realize that there will be a collection of forms and model code that will be duplicated in the dozen ActiveRecord models already in your application.

What are some strategies you can employ for reducing duplication and bloated Active Record models? What are the pros/cons of each strategy?

Because Ruby on Rails is an MVC framework, it can become tempting to try and fit everything into the Model or the Controller. Ruby on Rails is a powerful framework that provides many different mechanisms for describing our application and keeping our models and controllers nice and tidy.

Below are two ways of reducing fat models. They illustrate different levels of shared understanding between the extracted functionality and the model in question.

1. Use ActiveSupport::Concern
If the code really belongs in the model (because it relies on ActiveRecord helpers), but there is a coherent grouping of methods, a concern might be worth implementing. For example, many models in a system could enable a user to create a note on a number of models:

require 'active_support/concern'

module Concerns::Noteable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_many :notes, as: :noteable, dependent: :destroy
  end

  def has_simple_notes?
    notes.not_reminders_or_todos.any?
  end

  def has_to_do_notes?
    notes.to_dos.any?
  end

  def has_reminder_notes?
    notes.reminders.any?
  end
  ...
end
The Concern can then be applied like so:

class Language < ActiveRecord::Base
  include TryFind
  include Concerns::Noteable
end
Pros:
This is a great way of testing a cohesive piece of functionality and making it clear to other developers that these methods belong together. Unit tests can also operate on a test double or a stub, which will keep functionality as decoupled from the remaining model implementation as possible.

Cons:
ActiveSupport::Concerns can be a bit controversial. When they are over-used, the model becomes peppered in multiple files and it’s possible for multiple concerns to have clashing implementations. A concern is still fundamentally coupled to Rails.

2. Delegate
Depending on the source of the bloat, sometimes it makes better sense to delegate to a service class. 10 lines of validation code can be wrapped up in a custom validator and tucked away in app/validators. Transformation of form parameters can be placed in a custom form under app/forms. If you have custom business logic, it may be prudent to keep it in a lib/ folder until it’s well defined.

The beauty of delegation is that the service classes will have no knowledge of the business domain and can be safely refactored and tested without any knowledge of the models.

Pros:
This approach is elegant and builds a custom library on top of what Ruby on Rails provides out of the box.

Cons:
If the underlying APIs change, your code will likely need to be updated to match. Instead of coupling to your model layer, you’ve now coupled yourself to either Ruby on Rails or a third-party library.

Conclusion :
This question helps demonstrate two critical skills every Ruby developer needs to develop: how to handle complexity from emerging requirements and how to decide the most appropriate refactoring.

By working through different refactoring strategies, you can explore a candidate’s problem-solving skills, their overall familiarity with Ruby on Rails, and their knowledge of MVC. Knowing what code is specific to the application and what can be generalized into a completely decoupled piece of functionality is important.
directAnswer: For notes shared across many models, use a polymorphic Note association with a cohesive Noteable concern, or delegate a workflow to a service/form object when it crosses model boundaries.
explanation: A concern removes duplicated association/helpers but remains coupled to its host models and can conceal responsibilities when overused. Delegation/composition makes dependencies and workflow boundaries explicit but adds interfaces to maintain. Keep view markup in shared partials and validation rules in cohesive validators. A service can legitimately know the business domain; it need not be a domain-agnostic utility.
example:
module Noteable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  included do
    has_many :notes, as: :noteable, dependent: :destroy
  end
end
class Note < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :noteable, polymorphic: true
end
class Product < ApplicationRecord
  include Noteable
end
issues: Source claim that service classes have no business-domain knowledge is not a requirement and is often incorrect.
Design guidance is not a framework rule: domain models need not all persist, and services commonly encapsulate business-domain workflows.

question: Given an array [1,2,34,5,6,7,8,9], sum it up using a method:
directAnswer: Use Array#sum, or inject with an explicit zero accumulator; the supplied array sums to 72.
explanation: sum is the clearest numeric API. inject(0, :+) also returns zero for empty input, unlike inject(:+), which returns nil. Decide whether elements must all be numeric and whether exact Integer/Rational/BigDecimal arithmetic is required.
example:
def sum_numbers(array)
  array.sum
end
sum_numbers([1, 2, 34, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]) # 72
sum_numbers([]) # 0
issues: Source edge case: inject(:+) returns nil for an empty array.

question: What is metaprogramming?
sourceAnswer:
Ruby developers should know what metaprogramming is because it is widely used, especially in popular frameworks such as Rails, Sinatra, and Padrino. By using metaprogramming, you can reduce duplicate code. However, the downside is that it increases the complexity of the code in the long run.

Here’s an example of metaprogramming in Ruby:

A user can have a lot of roles, and you want to check the authorization.

Normal scenario:

def admin?
     role ==  'admin'
end

def marketer?
    role == 'marketer'
end

def sales?
   role == 'sales'
end
Metaprogramming:

['admin', 'marketer', 'sales'].each do |user_role|
    define_method "#{user_role}?" do
        role == user_role
    end
end
directAnswer: Metaprogramming means defining or adapting program behavior using code, often at runtime in Ruby.
explanation: define_method creates methods, class_eval/module_eval evaluates in a class/module context, and method_missing can handle unknown calls. Prefer explicit generated methods when the set is known; pair method_missing with respond_to_missing?. Avoid evaluating user input or exposing arbitrary method dispatch.

question: Give the output of the stated class implementation:
sourceAnswer:
Given this Human class implementation:

class Human

    def talk
        puts "I’m talking"
    end

     private

     def whisper
          puts "I’m whispering"
     end
end
What’s the output of:

Human.new.talk
Human.new.whisper
Human.new.send(:talk)
Human.new.send(:whisper)
I’m talking
NoMethodError: private method ‘whisper’ called for #<Human:0x007fd97b292d48>
I’m talking
I’m whispering
To explain, the class object Human.new.talk is calling an instance method, so it works perfectly. The talk method is a public method and can be called by everyone.

The class object Human.new.whisper is trying to access a private method, which it is not allowed to. Private and Protected methods are not accessible from outside. They are only used internally. This is an object-oriented design and can be used to structure the code, which the implementation is not supposed to expose to consumer object.

Finally, Human.new.send(:talk) sends a bypass control check to the method so it can be called without raising an error. Same goes to Human.new.send(:whisper).
directAnswer: Called independently: talk prints “I’m talking”; whisper raises NoMethodError; send(:talk) prints the public message; send(:whisper) invokes the private method and prints its message.
explanation: send bypasses ordinary method visibility; public_send respects it. If the four statements run sequentially without rescuing the second statement, execution stops at that exception and the later sends do not run. This is not a security sandbox, and an instance is not a “class object”.
example:
class Human
  def talk = puts("I’m talking")
  private
  def whisper = puts("I’m whispering")
end
h = Human.new
h.talk
begin
  h.whisper
rescue NoMethodError
  puts "private call rejected"
end
h.send(:talk)
h.send(:whisper)
issues: Source prints four independent outcomes without noting that the unrescued exception stops sequential execution.

question: Write code that splits a given array of integers into two arrays; the first containing odd numbers and second containing even numbers.
sourceAnswer:
%i|select reject|.map { |m| array.partition(&odd?)}
or

array.each_with_object({odd:[], even:[]}) do |elem, memo|
  memo[elem.odd? ? :odd : :even] << elem
end # inject for ruby < 2.0 is fine as well
The straightforward approach would be to call array.select to store odds and then array.reject to store evens. There is nothing wrong with this, except it violates DRY principle:

odds = array.select &:odd?
evens = array.reject &:odd?
Future modification of this code might accidentally change the only one line from the above pair, breaking consistency. It is not likely the case for this particular example, but DRY usually works for future use.

One might notice that the latter example does one iteration through an array, while the former is still iterating the array twice, once for each method. In most cases, the performance penalty is not significant, but it should be taken into consideration when dealing with huge arrays.

explanation: partition returns two arrays preserving encounter order. The first contains elements for which the block is truthy; the second contains the rest. This uses O(n) time and O(n) result storage. The source map/partition expression is malformed and ignores its iterator variable.

question: How would you flatten the following?
sourceAnswer:
hash = { a: { b: { c: 42, d: 'foo' }, d: 'bar' }, e: 'baz' }
to

{ :a_b_c=>42, :a_b_d=>"foo", :a_d=>"bar", :e=>"baz" }
λ = ->(h, key = nil) do
  h.map do |k, v|
    _k = key ? "#{key}_#{k}" : k.to_s
    v.is_a?(Hash) ? λ.call(v, _k) : [_k.to_sym, v]
  end.flatten #⇒ note flatten 
end
Hash[*λ.call(hash)]
#⇒ {:a_b_c=>42, :a_b_d=>"foo", :a_d=>"bar", :e=>"baz"}
Understanding recursion is important. While all these Fibonacci numbers and factorials are repeated over and over again, the real-world tasks are less academic. Walking through the hash in the described manner is often a must.

The exercise might be stated as the exact opposite: given the “flattened” form of the hash, rebuild its nested representation.
directAnswer: Recursively walk the nested hash and join the key path for each leaf. Preserve array-valued leaves instead of flattening them accidentally.
explanation: The source Array#flatten-based approach can corrupt array-valued leaf data. Joining paths with underscores is ambiguous if original keys contain underscores, so specify an escaping rule or keep path arrays for reversible flattening. Detect collisions rather than silently replacing values. Unflattening requires a defined conflict policy for a value at both a and a_b.
example:
def flatten_hash(hash, prefix = [], out = {})
  hash.each do |key, value|
    parts = prefix + [key.to_s]
    if value.is_a?(Hash)
      flatten_hash(value, parts, out)
    else
      joined = parts.join("_").to_sym
      raise ArgumentError, "key collision" if out.key?(joined)
      out[joined] = value
    end
  end
  out
end
flatten_hash({a: {b: {c: 42, d: "foo"}, d: "bar"}, e: "baz"})
# {:a_b_c=>42, :a_b_d=>"foo", :a_d=>"bar", :e=>"baz"}
importantPoints: For a reversible alternative, represent paths as arrays of keys rather than concatenated strings.
issues: Source reverse-flattening follow-up is under-specified without key escaping/collision rules.

question: Consider the following:
sourceAnswer:
Given the following syntactic sugar:

(1..42).reduce &:*
#⇒ 1405006117752879898543142606244511569936384000000000
What makes this notation to be an equivalent of:

(1..42).reduce { |memo, elem| memo * elem }
Does the Ruby parser handle this particular case, or could this be implemented in plain Ruby?

The candidate can monkeypatch to the Symbol class with their own implementation of the aforementioned syntactic sugar.

E.g.

class Symbol
def to_proc
  # this implementation in incomplete
  # — more sophisticated question: why?
  # — even more hard: re-implement it properly
lambda { |memo, recv| memo.public_send(self, recv)  }
end
end
(1..42).reduce &:*
#⇒ 1405006117752879898543142606244511569936384000000000
There is not much magic in this example. An ampersand converts an argument, that is apparently a Symbol instance here, to Proc object, simply calling to_proc method on it. The implementation is Symbol#to_proc in done in C for performance reasons, but the candidate can write their own implementation in Ruby to make sure everything works as expected.

Answers to additional questions in the code: — the code above fails when the callee expects to receive one parameter only

(e.g. a try to use this implementation with Enumerator#each)

will fail with an arity error:

(1..42).each &:*
ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (given 1, expected 2)
To fix this, the candidate should use the splat argument to lambda and analyze the amount of actual argument passed:

lambda do |*args|
  case args.size
  when 1 then # each-like
when 2 then # with accumulator
...
directAnswer: & converts the supplied object through to_proc; Symbol#to_proc creates a callable that sends that symbol-named method to its first argument.
explanation: For reduce(&:*) the accumulator is the receiver and the next element is the multiplication argument. A two-positional-argument lambda is not a general Symbol#to_proc replacement. The correct method forwarding shape needs a receiver plus arbitrary positional arguments, keywords and a block; exact arity/introspection/visibility details also matter. Do not globally monkey-patch Symbol just to solve the exercise.
issues: Source inference: calling (1..42).each(&:*) is invalid even with the genuine Symbol#to_proc because Integer#* still requires an argument; it is not a valid positive test of a repaired converter.

question: What’s wrong with the code below and why?
sourceAnswer:
require 'benchmark'
puts Benchmark.measure do  
    break if Random.rand(100) === 1 while true
end
Operator precedence matters! The code will return

LocalJumpError: no block given (yield)
As do-end is weaker than attracting arguments to the function, that’s why one either needs to surround the whole call to Benchmark.measure with parentheses, or to use curly brackets instead of do-end.
directAnswer: The do/end block binds to puts, so Benchmark.measure receives no block and raises LocalJumpError. Parenthesize the measured call or use braces.
explanation: Ruby block-binding precedence makes braces bind more tightly than do/end in this call form. Benchmark.measure yields to a supplied block; it cannot measure the loop if the block belongs to puts. A deterministic bounded operation is a better repeatable timing example than a random infinite loop.

question: Build an array based on the following scenario.
sourceAnswer:
Provided we have a hash of a fixed structure (e. g. we receive this hash from a third-party data provider, that guarantees the structure):

input = [	{a1: 42, b1: { c1: 'foo' }}, 
{a2: 43, b2: { c2: 'bar' }}, 
{a3: 44, b3: { c3: 'baz' }},
… ]
How can one build an array of cN values (['foo', bar', baz'])?

Some examples would be:

input.map { |v| v.to_a.last.last.to_a.last.last }
or

input.map { |v| v.flatten.last.flatten.last }
Here one iterates through the array, collecting nested hashes and using an index to build the requested key name, but there is more straightforward approach. Hash is an Enumerable, which gives the developer an ability to query it almost as what has been done with an array.
directAnswer: With the stated aN/bN/cN key convention, use map and dig with the position-derived keys to obtain the nested values.
explanation: Do not infer meaning from a hash’s last inserted key when the schema names are known. Confirm whether keys are symbols or strings and whether keys may be missing; dig returns nil for a missing path but can raise if an intermediate value does not support dig. The input guarantee matters more than a short flatten/to_a trick.
example:
input = [{a1: 42, b1: {c1: "foo"}}, {a2: 43, b2: {c2: "bar"}}, {a3: 44, b3: {c3: "baz"}}]
values = input.each_with_index.map do |row, index|
  n = index + 1
  row.dig("b#{n}".to_sym, "c#{n}".to_sym)
end
values # ["foo", "bar", "baz"]
issues: The source index-free flattening examples depend on insertion order and can silently extract the wrong data.

question: Consider the following scenario related to variables.
sourceAnswer:
Given the code below, how one might access the @foo variable from outside? Is it an instance variable, or class variable? What object this variable is defined on?

class Foo
  class << self
    @foo = 42
  end
end
You can access the variable with

(class << Foo ; @foo ; end)
It’s an instance variable and defined on Foo’s Singleton method, or more specifically, the eigenclass of Foo.

Each class in Ruby has its own “eigenclass.” This eigenclass is derived from Class class. Foo class is an instance of it’s eigenclass. This eigenclass has the only instance Foo; it as well has instance methods, defined as class methods on Foo, and it might have instance variables, e. g. @foo variable in this particular example.
directAnswer: Inside class << self, self is Foo’s singleton class, so @foo belongs to that singleton-class object, not to an instance of Foo and not to Foo itself.
explanation: Read it with Foo.singleton_class.instance_variable_get(:@foo), or execute a class << Foo body. A class object has a singleton class in its method lookup path, but Foo.class is Class; describing Foo as the sole instance of its eigenclass is a misleading account of Ruby class membership.
example:
class Foo
  class << self
    @foo = 42
  end
end
Foo.singleton_class.instance_variable_get(:@foo) # 42
Foo.instance_variable_get(:@foo) # nil
Foo.class # Class
issues: Corrected the source’s inaccurate eigenclass/class-membership explanation.
The singleton-class body stores @foo on the eigenclass object. Foo remains an instance of Class; singleton lookup is distinct from ordinary class membership.

question: What are the different uses of Ruby modules? Could you provide an example of each and explain why it is valuable?
sourceAnswer:
Traits/Mixins:
Examples: Mappable, Renderable, Movable
Traits/Mixins is a useful alternative to class inheritance when there is a need to acquire behavior that describes a trait (e.g. Renderable) instead of an is-a relationship (e.g. Vehicle), especially when there is a need for multiple traits since a class can only inherit once.
Namespace:
Examples: Graphics, Devise, Finance
Namespace Ruby classes and modules to avoid naming clashes with similarly-named classes/modules from libraries
Singleton class alternative:
Examples: Application, Universe, Game
Modules cannot be instantiated, therefore they can be used as an easy alternative to singleton classes to represent only one instance of a domain model via module methods (equivalent of class methods)
Bag of stateless helper methods:
Examples: Helpers, Math, Physics
Stateless helper methods receive their data via arguments without needing a class to be instantiated nor keep any state (e.g. calculate_interest(amount, rate_per_year, period)), so a module is used instead for holding a bag of stateless helper methods.
In addition to knowing the 4 different functions of modules in Ruby cited above, it’s important that your candidate knows when to use a module v.s. a superclass when doing object-oriented domain modeling. This can greatly impact the maintenance of the code a few months down the road in a software project.

For another practical example, a car-race-betting game allows players to bet on cars rendered on the screen as moving at different speeds. Players can print a sheet of game results representing each car’s details and status to claim their prize at a casino when the game is over.

If the candidate were to implement all of these details in a car object, and later introduce differences between a Jaguar, Mercedez, and Porche, the candidate would rely on a car superclass shared among three subclasses via inheritance.

However, if in the future, trucks and horses are thrown into the mix as well, the candidate would have to split the ability of an object to move, the ability to render object on screen, and the ability to print object details into separate modules (Movable, Renderable, and Printable respectively), and mix them into each of Car, Truck, and Horse.

Next, the three classes can each serve as a superclass for multiple subtypes as needed by the game (e.g. JaguarCar, FireTruck, ThoroughbredHorse). This will offer maximum separation of concerns and improved maintainability of the code.
directAnswer: Modules provide namespaces, reusable mixin behavior and module-level utility interfaces without requiring multiple class inheritance.
explanation: Use inheritance for a substitutable is-a relationship and mixins/composition for shared capabilities. A module can hold state and module methods, but it is not automatically equivalent to a carefully designed singleton service. Keep dependencies and method collisions visible, especially when many modules are included.
example:
module Graphics
  class Canvas; end
end
module Printable
  def print_label = "printable"
end
class Car
  include Printable
end
Car.new.print_label

question: Explain MVC architecture in Ruby on Rails with an example.
directAnswer: MVC separates domain/data behavior in models, presentation in views, and request coordination in controllers.
explanation: The router dispatches a request to a controller action. The action loads or changes domain objects and renders a view or another representation, or returns a redirect. Active Record models often provide persistence, but a model need not inherit from Active Record. Views should avoid database queries, and complex workflows can live in services or other domain objects.

# app/controllers/posts_controller.rb def show @post = Post.find(params[:id]) end # app/views/posts/show.html.erb

<%= @post.title %>

question: What does “everything is an object” mean in Ruby?
directAnswer: Ruby values such as numbers, nil, booleans, classes and modules are objects; syntax constructs such as if and def are not themselves ordinary value objects.
explanation: Every object has a class and identity and receives method calls. Class is itself a class, classes are objects, and BasicObject is the minimal root of the normal hierarchy. A block is syntax that can be captured in a Proc; do not claim every language keyword or raw block is an object.
example:
1.class # Integer
nil.class # NilClass
String.class # Class
Class.superclass # Module

question: How does Rails handle routing and request flow?
directAnswer: A request passes through the web server and Rack middleware, the router chooses a controller action, callbacks and the action run, then Rails returns a response.
explanation: The action can call models/services and render HTML, JSON or another representation, send headers, or redirect. A redirect asks the client to make another request. Routes decide allowed verbs; actions are not automatically GET endpoints. Authentication, authorization, CSRF and error handling apply at the relevant boundaries.
example: GET /posts/7 → Rack middleware → router → PostsController#show → Post.find(7) → show.html.erb → HTTP response

question: How can you achieve multiple inheritance in Ruby?
directAnswer: Ruby classes have one superclass; modules provide namespaces and reusable mixin behavior through include, prepend or extend.
explanation: include adds module methods to an instance lookup chain, prepend places them before the class, and extend adds them to a particular object’s singleton class. A plain module cannot be instantiated with new. Mixins reuse behavior but are not multiple class inheritance.
example:
module Printable
  def print_label = "label"
end
class Product
  include Printable
end
Product.new.print_label

question: What is the difference between symbols and strings?
directAnswer: A Symbol is an immutable identifier value; a String is a text value that is normally mutable unless frozen.
explanation: Symbols with the same name refer to the same symbol object within the runtime. String identity depends on creation, interning and freezing, so object IDs are not a general type definition. Since Ruby 2.2 many dynamically created symbols can be garbage collected; symbols are not universally permanent memory leaks. Use strings for user content and symbols for a bounded vocabulary of names.
example:
:name == :name # true
"name" == :name # false
"name".to_sym # :name
:name.to_s # "name"

question: What does self mean in Ruby?
sourceAnswer: Database and Active Record
directAnswer: self is the current receiver; it changes with execution context.
explanation: Inside an instance method self is that instance. In a class body or class method it is the class object. self is often used when assigning through a setter, or defining a singleton/class method. Calling another class method from a class method does not always require an explicit self receiver.
example:
class User
  def self.kind = self
  def receiver = self
end
User.kind # User
User.new.receiver # the instance

question: How do Active Record associations work?
directAnswer: Associations describe model relationships using belongs_to, has_one, has_many, has_many :through, has_one :through, or has_and_belongs_to_many.
explanation: A belongs_to normally places the foreign key on the declaring model; has_many places it on the associated rows. belongs_to alone does not imply a one-to-one relationship. Use a unique foreign-key index for a true one-to-one relationship. Migrations must create the required columns and constraints; declaring association macros alone does not alter the schema.
example:
class Author < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :books
end
class Book < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :author
end
# books.author_id references authors.id

question: What are database transactions and how are they implemented in Rails?
directAnswer: Wrap related writes in an Active Record transaction so they commit together or roll back together on failure.
explanation: Use bang persistence methods when invalid data must abort the block; save returning false alone does not automatically roll back earlier writes. Transactions are scoped to a database connection, not an atomic unit across unrelated databases or external APIs. ActiveRecord::Rollback rolls back without escaping the block. Run external side effects after commit or through an outbox.
example:
ApplicationRecord.transaction do
  user.save!
  order.save!
end
importantPoints: Nested transactions normally join the outer transaction; requires_new: true uses a savepoint where supported.

question: How do you optimize database queries in Rails applications?
sourceAnswer: Performance and Scalability
directAnswer: Measure the query and request first, then reduce unnecessary rows/work, fix N+1 access, and add indexes justified by the query plan.
explanation: Use SQL logs and database EXPLAIN, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a suitable environment, to inspect scans, joins, estimates and sorts. Select needed columns, paginate, batch writes and avoid repeated queries. Check query count and latency before and after the change. Caching can help repeated reads but should not hide an incorrect query or stale authorization boundary.
example:
User.where(active: true).order(:id).limit(100).pluck(:id, :email)
# Inspect the generated SQL and plan before adding an index.

question: How do you analyze performance issues in a Rails application?

question: What is a class?
sourceAnswer:
A text-book answer: classes are a blue-print for constructing computer models for real or virtual objects... boring.

In reality: classes hold **data**, have **methods** that interact with that data, and are used to **instantiate objects**.

Like this.

```ruby
class WhatAreClasses
  def initialize
    @data = "I'm instance data of this object. Hello."
  end

  def method
    puts @data.gsub("instance", "altered")
  end
end

object = WhatAreClasses.new
object.method
 #=> I'm altered data of this object. Hello.
```
directAnswer: A class is an object defining the behavior and construction of its instances.
explanation: Instance methods define behavior for each instance; each object has its own instance-variable state. Classes can themselves have singleton methods and instance variables. Class.new constructs new anonymous classes; SomeClass.new allocates an instance and invokes initialize.
example:
class User
  attr_reader :name
  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end
end
User.new("Ada").name

question: What is an object?
sourceAnswer:
An instance of a class.  

To some, it's also the root class in ruby (Object).

Classes themselves descend from the Object root class. (Kudos to Ezra)
directAnswer: An object is a value with identity, class membership and behavior; it can also hold state in instance variables.
explanation: Object is a particular class, not the general definition of an object. In modern Ruby, BasicObject is the minimal root, while most ordinary objects inherit from Object. Classes and modules are also objects.
example:
user = Object.new
user.class # Object
user.object_id # identity, not a portable raw memory address
issues: Modern Ruby has BasicObject as the minimal root; Object is the usual root for ordinary application objects.

question: What is a module?  Can you tell me the difference between classes and modules?
sourceAnswer:
Modules serve as a mechanism for **namespaces**.

```ruby
module ANamespace
  class AClass
    def initialize
      puts "Another object, coming right up!"
    end
  end
end

ANamespace::AClass.new
 #=> Another object, coming right up!
```

Also, modules provide as a mechanism for multiple inheritance via **mix-ins** and **cannot be instantiated** like classes can.

```ruby
module AMixIn
  def who_am_i?
    puts "An existentialist, that's who."
  end
end

# String is already the parent class
class DeepString < String
  # extend adds instance methods from AMixIn as class methods
  extend AMixIn
end

DeepString.who_am_i?
 #=> An existentialist, that's who.

AMixIn.new
 #=> NoMethodError: undefined method ‘new’ for AMixIn:Module
```
directAnswer: Ruby classes have one superclass; modules provide namespaces and reusable mixin behavior through include, prepend or extend.
explanation: include adds module methods to an instance lookup chain, prepend places them before the class, and extend adds them to a particular object’s singleton class. A plain module cannot be instantiated with new. Mixins reuse behavior but are not multiple class inheritance.
example:
module Printable
  def print_label = "label"
end
class Product
  include Printable
end
Product.new.print_label

question: Can you tell me the three levels of method access control for classes and modules?  What do they imply about the method?
sourceAnswer:
**All methods**, no matter the access control, can be **accessed within the class**.  But what about outside callers?

_Public_ methods enforce **no access control** -- they can be called in any scope.

_Protected_ methods are only accessible to **other objects of the same class**.

_Private_ methods are only accessible within the **context of the current object**.

```ruby
class AccessLevel
  def something_interesting
    another = AccessLevel.new
    another.public_method
    another.protected_method
    another.private_method
  end

  def public_method
    puts "Public method. Nice to meet you."
  end

  protected

  def protected_method
    puts "Protected method. Sweet!"
  end

  private 

  def private_method
    puts "Incoming exception!"
  end
end

AccessLevel.new.something_interesting
 #=> Public method.  Nice to meet you.
 #=> Protected method.  Sweet!
 #=> NoMethodError: private method ‘private_method’ called for
 #=>  #<AccessLevel:0x898c8>
```
directAnswer: Ruby methods can be public, protected or private; visibility controls ordinary method-call access rather than object security.
explanation: Public methods accept ordinary explicit receivers. Protected methods may be called with an explicit compatible receiver from the defining class/subclass context. Private methods normally use an implicit receiver; modern Ruby permits literal self in private calls. send bypasses visibility; public_send enforces public access. Instance methods are usually public by default, while initialize is private.
example:
class Account
  def visible = balance
  private
  def balance = 10
end
Account.new.visible # 10
Account.new.public_send(:balance) # raises NoMethodError
issues: Visibility and class-variable sharing require precise Ruby context/inheritance rules; see corrected answer rather than the source’s simplified class-only statement.

question: There are four ways to invoke a method in ruby.  Can you give me at least two?
sourceAnswer:
Here, I'm looking for either the **dot operator** (or period operator), the **Object#send** method, the **method(:name).call** method, or the **double colon operator**.

Strong candidates will be able to speak about the importance of code consistency. And the strongest candidates will mention how consistency can be achived by adhering to a [Ruby style guide](https://rubystyle.guide) with [linting and formating tools](https://rubocop.org/).

```ruby
object = Object.new
puts object.object_id
 #=> 282660

puts object.send(:object_id)

puts object.method(:object_id).call # (Kudos to Ezra)

puts object::object_id # (Kudos to OrestF)

```

## Separating the professional from the hobbyist

Senior programmers _should_ be able to give competent answers for all questions.  Junior programmers _should_ answer some correct, but usually won't know them all.
directAnswer: A Ruby method call sends a message to a receiver; lookup searches the receiver’s method lookup chain and invokes method_missing if no matching method is found.
explanation: Methods can be invoked with normal dot syntax, public_send/send, or a Method object’s call. Respect visibility and do not pass arbitrary untrusted method names to send. A method object captures a receiver, while source code syntax alone does not.
example:
user.name
user.public_send(:name)
user.method(:name).call
# send can invoke private methods, so it is not equivalent to public_send.

question: Explain this ruby idiom: a ||= b
sourceAnswer:
A common idiom that strong ruby developers use all the time.

```ruby
# a = b when a == false
# otherwise a remains unchanged
a = a || b
```

```ruby
a = 1
b = 2
a ||= b #=> a = 1
```

```ruby
a = nil
b = 2
a ||= b #=> a = 2
```

```ruby
a = false
b = 2
a ||= b #=> a = 2
```
directAnswer: a ||= b assigns b only when a is nil or false; a truthy value such as 0 is preserved.
explanation: It is useful for defaulting/memoization but cannot cache a legitimate false/nil result without another sentinel. With indexed or accessor assignment, the language’s evaluation/assignment behavior is more precise than simply copying a = a || b. It is not an atomic cross-thread initialization primitive.
example:
a = false
a ||= 2 # a becomes 2
a = 0
a ||= 2 # a stays 0

question: What does self mean?
sourceAnswer:
`self` _always_ refers to the current object.  But this question is more difficult than it seems because **Classes are also objects** in ruby.  (Kudos to Stephen)

```ruby
class WhatIsSelf
  def test
    puts "At the instance level, self is #{self}"
  end

  def self.test
    puts "At the class level, self is #{self}"
  end
end

WhatIsSelf.test 
 #=> At the class level, self is WhatIsSelf

WhatIsSelf.new.test 
 #=> At the instance level, self is #<WhatIsSelf:0x28190>
```

This short snippet indicates two things:

- at the _class level_, self is the **class**, in this case WhatIsSelf.
- at the _instance level_, self is the **instance in context**, in this case the instance of WhatIsSelf at memory location 0x28190.
directAnswer: self is the current receiver; it changes with execution context.
explanation: Inside an instance method self is that instance. In a class body or class method it is the class object. self is often used when assigning through a setter, or defining a singleton/class method. Calling another class method from a class method does not always require an explicit self receiver.
example:
class User
  def self.kind = self
  def receiver = self
end
User.kind # User
User.new.receiver # the instance

question: What is a Proc?
sourceAnswer:
Everyone usually confuses procs with blocks, but the strongest rubyist can grok the true meaning of the question.

Essentially, Procs are **anonymous methods** (or nameless functions) containing code. They can be placed inside a variable and **passed around** like any other object or scalar value. They are created by **Proc.new**, **lambda**, and **blocks** (invoked by the yield keyword).  

**Note:** Procs and lambdas do have subtle, but important, [differences](http://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Ruby_Programming/Syntax/Method_Calls#Understanding_blocks.2C_Procs_and_methods) in ruby v1.8.6.  However, I wouldn't expect a candidate talk about these nitty-gritty details during an interview. (Kudos to Noah Thorp)

```ruby
# wants a proc, a lambda, AND a block
def three_ways(proc, lambda, &block)
  proc.call
  lambda.call
  yield # like block.call
  puts "#{proc.inspect} #{lambda.inspect} #{block.inspect}"
end

anonymous = Proc.new { puts "I'm a Proc for sure." }
nameless  = lambda { puts "But what about me?" }

three_ways(anonymous, nameless) do
  puts "I'm a block, but could it be???"
end
 #=> I'm a Proc for sure.
 #=> But what about me?
 #=> I'm a block, but could it be???
 #=> #<Proc:0x00089d64> #<Proc:0x00089c74> #<Proc:0x00089b34>
```
directAnswer: A Proc is a callable object capturing a block and its lexical context; a lambda is a Proc with method-like argument and return behavior.
explanation: A block is passed with braces or do/end and is not automatically a standalone object. Capture it with &block when an object is needed. Lambda return exits the lambda, while non-lambda Proc return attempts to exit its defining method and can raise LocalJumpError later. Lambdas check arity more strictly than ordinary procs. yield invokes the method’s supplied block; it does not by itself create a Proc.
example:
factor = 3
triple = ->(n) { n * factor }
triple.call(4) # 12
def with_value
  yield 10
end
with_value { |n| n + 1 } # 11
issues: Proc and lambda behavior matters in modern Ruby; raw blocks are not standalone objects and yield invokes a supplied block rather than creating a Proc.

question: What is unit testing (in classical terms)?  What is the primary technique when writing a test?
sourceAnswer:
The strongest candidates should be quite comfortable with test or behavior driven development.

Unit testing, simply put, is testing methods -- the smallest unit in object-oriented programming.  Strong candidates will argue that it allows a developer to flesh out their API before it's consumed by other systems in the application.

The primary way to achieve this is to **assert** that the **actual** result of the method matches an **expected** result.

```ruby
require "test/unit"

class Brokened
  def uh_oh
    "I needs fixing"
  end
end

class BrokenedTest < Test::Unit::TestCase
  def test_uh_oh
    actual = Brokened.new
    assert_equal("I'm all better!", actual.uh_oh)
  end
end
 #=> Started
 #=> F
 #=> Finished in 0.663831 seconds.
 #=> 
 #=>   1) Failure:
 #=> test_uh_oh:11
 #=> <"I'm all better!"> expected but was
 #=> <"I needs fixing">.
 #=> 
 #=> 1 tests, 1 assertions, 1 failures, 0 errors
```

## Show me the money!

Variable typing is one of those topics that everyone sort of understands it, but is hard to put it into words.  I've iterated and improved the next series of questions to really test a **senior level** candidate's knowledge of static and dynamic typing.  This is my best attempt so far.

question: What does this say about the advantages of ruby's dynamic (duck) typed system?

explanation: Duck typing depends on the behavior an object supports rather than requiring a particular class. Use tests, contracts and optional static typing tools where they help, and profile performance rather than assuming every dynamic program is slower.

question: What is Garbage collection in ruby on Rails?

Also, the users can relax on tracking the objects again and again in the long run. All the objects which are no longer required can directly be moved from the memory with this approach.

explanation: MRI uses tracing, generational and incremental collection, with implementation/version-specific compaction behavior. GC operates during the process lifetime, not only when a program ends. Retained references, native allocations and allocator fragmentation can all cause high memory use. example:
before = GC.stat(:total_allocated_objects)
1000.times { Object.new }

question: What is the use of load and require in Ruby?

question: Explain case statement in Ruby.

example:

when 0..17 then "minor"

end

question: Explain for loop in Ruby.

question: Explain do while loop in Ruby.

example:
n = 0
loop do
  n += 1
  break if n >= 3
end

question: Explain until loop in Ruby.
sourceAnswer: Ruby until loop runs until the given condition evaluates to true. It exits the loop when condition becomes true. It is opposite of the while loop.
directAnswer: until repeats its body while the condition is falsey and stops once the condition is truthy.
explanation: Use it when the positive end condition is easier to understand than a negated while. Like while it can execute zero times when the condition is already satisfied.
example:
n = 0
until n == 3
  n += 1
end

question: Explain break statement in Ruby.

directAnswer: break exits the enclosing loop or iterator and may supply its result value.
explanation: next skips the remainder of one iteration; redo restarts the same iteration; return exits a method. Proc/lambda context affects nonlocal control-flow behavior, so do not treat them as interchangeable.

result # 2

question: What are migrations in Rails?
sourceAnswer:
Migrations in Rails are a way to manage and version database schema changes. They allow you to create, modify, and delete database tables and columns over time, ensuring that your schema changes are consistent and trackable. Migrations are written as Ruby classes and are run with commands like rails db:migrate. Each migration file includes methods to define changes (up method) and revert them (down method). For example:

class AddAgeToUsers < ActiveRecord::Migration[6.1]
  def change
    add_column :users, :age, :integer
  end
end
directAnswer: Migrations are versioned Ruby schema changes; run bin/rails db:migrate to apply them and bin/rails db:rollback to undo the latest reversible migration.
explanation: Use change for reversible operations, or up/down/reversible when Rails cannot infer reversal. Rails records applied migration versions in schema_migrations and maintains schema.rb or structure.sql. Do not edit already-applied migrations to change production schema. Adapter-specific SQL and some DDL cannot be portable or reversible, and rollback may lose data.
example:
bin/rails generate migration AddAgeToUsers age:integer
# Generated class version matches the app:
def change
  add_column :users, :age, :integer
end
bin/rails db:migrate
importantPoints: ruby script/generate and class-level self.up/self.down examples are legacy syntax; modern migrations normally use versioned classes and instance methods.

question: How does Rails handle database transactions?
sourceAnswer:
Rails handles database transactions using Active Record's transaction methods, which ensure that a series of database operations are executed as a single unit of work. If any part of the transaction fails, all changes are rolled back to maintain data integrity. For example:

ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
  user = User.create!(name: 'John Doe')
  profile = Profile.create!(user: user, bio: 'Developer')
  # If an error occurs here, both user and profile will be rolled back
end
The ActiveRecord::Base.transaction block wraps two create! operations. If any of these operations fail, the entire transaction is rolled back, and neither user nor profile will be saved to the database.
directAnswer: Wrap related writes in an Active Record transaction so they commit together or roll back together on failure.
explanation: Use bang persistence methods when invalid data must abort the block; save returning false alone does not automatically roll back earlier writes. Transactions are scoped to a database connection, not an atomic unit across unrelated databases or external APIs. ActiveRecord::Rollback rolls back without escaping the block. Run external side effects after commit or through an outbox.
example:
ApplicationRecord.transaction do
  user.save!
  order.save!
end
importantPoints: Nested transactions normally join the outer transaction; requires_new: true uses a savepoint where supported.

  validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true
end

user = User.new(email: 'test@example.com')
user.save
puts User.count
Answer: The output is 1 because the code creates and saves a new User instance with a unique email. After saving, it prints the total count of User records in the database, which is 1 since one user has been successfully added.
directAnswer: The output is the total number of rows after the save attempt; it is 1 only under extra assumptions such as an initially empty table and a successful save.
explanation: A uniqueness validator can prevent the new record from saving if a row with that email already exists. Other validations/callbacks can also fail or database writes can raise. The code provides no initial database state, so an unconditional numeric answer is impossible. Check save’s result or use save! when failure must raise.
example:
before = User.count
user = User.new(email: "test@example.com")
if user.save
  puts "count increased by one: #{User.count == before + 1}"
else
  puts user.errors.full_messages
end

question: What is the difference between find and find_by in Rails?
sourceAnswer:
In Rails, find and find_by are methods used to retrieve records from the database, but they serve different purposes. find is used to locate a record by its primary key (usually the id). It raises an ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound exception if the record with the given primary key does not exist. For example, User.find(1) will fetch the user with an id of 1, or throw an error if no such user exists.

find_by, on the other hand, allows you to query records using any attribute, not just the primary key. It returns the first record that matches the given conditions or nil if no record is found. For instance, User.find_by(email: 'example@example.com') will find the first user with the specified email or return nil if no such user exists.
directAnswer: find retrieves by primary key and raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound when missing; find_by uses attribute conditions and returns one match or nil.
explanation: find_by! raises when no row matches. Without ordering, “first match” does not promise a business order. Dynamic finders such as find_by_email are convenience methods, but the explicit find_by(email: value) interface is clearer and easier to compose.
example:
User.find(42)
User.find_by(email: "dev@example.com")
User.find_by!(email: "dev@example.com")

question: Describe how Rails implements single-table inheritance (STI).
sourceAnswer:
Rails implements Single Table Inheritance (STI) by using a single database table to store records for multiple subclasses of a parent class. This approach allows different subclasses to inherit from a common base class while sharing the same table.

In STI, a special column, typically named type, is used in the database table to differentiate between the various subclasses. This column holds the name of the subclass, enabling Rails to instantiate the correct subclass when retrieving records from the table.
directAnswer: Single-table inheritance stores a base class and its subclasses in one table, usually using a type column to select the Ruby subclass.
explanation: Use it when subclasses truly share an is-a relationship and much of their schema. Unrelated types can create sparse tables, complicated validations and accidental type coupling. It differs from polymorphic associations, which link records of different models without making those models subclasses of a shared persisted type.
example:
class Vehicle < ApplicationRecord; end
class Car < Vehicle; end
class Truck < Vehicle; end
Car.create! # vehicles.type is "Car"

question: What is the purpose of the find_or_create_by method in Rails?
sourceAnswer:
The find_or_create_by method attempts to find a record with the given attributes; if none is found, it creates a new record with those attributes. This method simplifies the process of ensuring a record's existence without needing to manually check if it exists first. For example:

user = User.find_or_create_by(email: 'user@example.com')
directAnswer: find_or_create_by first looks up a matching row, then attempts creation if no match exists.
explanation: It can race between the read and insert. Enforce uniqueness in the database; choose find_or_create_by! when validation failure should raise. create_or_find_by is another option when a suitable database unique constraint is present, with its own insert-first trade-offs.
example:
add_index :users, :email, unique: true
# Application code:
User.find_or_create_by!(email: "dev@example.com")
importantPoints: A model uniqueness validation alone does not make concurrent creation safe.

question: How does Rails implement strong parameters, and why is it important?
sourceAnswer:
Rails implements strong parameters as a security feature to protect against mass assignment vulnerabilities. This feature ensures that only permitted attributes are allowed to be updated or created through mass assignment, such as when handling form submissions. This is crucial for preventing unintended changes to model attributes and ensuring that users can only modify what they are allowed to. For example:

def user_params
  params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email)
end
directAnswer: Strong Parameters allowlist attributes for mass assignment; they do not provide general value validation, authorization, or universal type casting.
explanation: Form and query parameters normally arrive as strings; JSON bodies can carry JSON types. Use require/permit, or expect in Rails 8+, to define the input shape. Validate values and authorize the target record separately. Do not permit role/admin or tenant ownership fields merely because the client sent them.
example:
def user_params
  params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email)
end
# Rails 8+: params.expect(user: [:name, :email])
# Ownership must still be checked: current_user.posts.find(params[:id])
importantPoints: Strong Parameters has been built into Rails since Rails 4; a separate strong_parameters gem was a historical backport.

question: How do Rails scopes work?
sourceAnswer:
In Rails, scopes are a way to define reusable queries that can be applied to ActiveRecord models. They help organize and encapsulate query logic, making it easier to write and maintain complex queries while keeping your models clean and readable. For example:

class Post < ApplicationRecord
  scope :published, -> { where(published: true) }
end
directAnswer: A scope is a named, composable query expressed as an Active Record relation.
explanation: Use a lambda for values that change with time so they are evaluated when the scope runs, rather than at class load. Scopes should return a relation; class methods are appropriate when logic is more complex. Avoid broad default scopes that unexpectedly affect writes or administrative queries.
example:
scope :recent, -> { where("created_at >= ?", 1.week.ago) }
Post.published.recent.order(:id)

question: What are Rails validations, and why are they important?
sourceAnswer:
Rails validations are mechanisms used to ensure that data being saved to the database meets specific criteria or constraints. They are a crucial part of the Rails framework, ensuring data integrity and consistency by enforcing rules at the application level before data is persisted. For example:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  # Presence validation
  validates :name, presence: true

  # Length validation
  validates :email, length: { minimum: 5 }

  # Uniqueness validation
  validates :email, uniqueness: true

  # Format validation
  validates :email, format: { with: URI::MailTo::EMAIL_REGEXP }
end


Expert-Level Ruby on Rails Interview Questions
Here are some expert-level interview questions for Ruby on Rails:
directAnswer: Model validations check whether an object meets application rules before normal persistence; database constraints enforce integrity across every writer.
explanation: Use validates for presence, length, numericality and other checks. valid? populates errors without saving. save returns false for validation failure; save! raises. Bulk SQL operations such as update_all bypass validations and callbacks, so important constraints must also exist in the database.
example:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  validates :name, presence: true
  validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true
end
user = User.new
user.valid? # false
user.errors.full_messages

question: How would you handle a scenario where you need to optimize a Rails application's performance due to slow database queries?
sourceAnswer:
To optimize performance, we can start by analyzing slow queries using tools like the EXPLAIN command or the Rails log for identifying bottlenecks. Consider adding appropriate indexes to the database tables and optimizing SQL queries.

Utilize caching mechanisms such as fragment caching, low-level caching, or Rails caching strategies to reduce the load on the database. Also, examine your Active Record associations and queries to ensure they are efficient and avoid N+1 query problems.
directAnswer: Measure the query and request first, then reduce unnecessary rows/work, fix N+1 access, and add indexes justified by the query plan.
explanation: Use SQL logs and database EXPLAIN, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a suitable environment, to inspect scans, joins, estimates and sorts. Select needed columns, paginate, batch writes and avoid repeated queries. Check query count and latency before and after the change. Caching can help repeated reads but should not hide an incorrect query or stale authorization boundary.
example:
User.where(active: true).order(:id).limit(100).pluck(:id, :email)
# Inspect the generated SQL and plan before adding an index.

question: Explain the concept of Service Objects in Rails.
sourceAnswer:
Service Objects in Rails are a design pattern used to organize and encapsulate business logic that doesn't naturally fit within the model or controller layers. They help maintain a clean separation of concerns, making the code more modular, readable, and maintainable. For example:

# Example: Service Object for processing payments
class PaymentService
  def initialize(user, amount)
    @user = user
    @amount = amount
  end

  def process
    # Payment processing logic
  end
end
directAnswer: A service object is a Ruby object representing an application operation, such as capturing a payment or importing a file.
explanation: It coordinates domain objects and explicit dependencies and gives the operation a testable boundary. Define transaction ownership, failure results, retries and idempotency deliberately. It is not a required Rails framework class. Service objects often know the business domain, contrary to the source claim that they must have no domain knowledge.
example:
class PublishPost
  def call(post)
    post.update!(published_at: Time.current)
    post
  end
end

question: Explain the purpose and use of Rails' Active Storage service.
sourceAnswer:
Active Storage integrates with Rails to manage file uploads and attachments directly within the framework. It supports direct uploads to cloud services like Amazon S3 and has built-in support for image processing. Unlike other gems, it is part of Rails and tightly integrated into the framework. For example:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_one_attached :avatar
end

# In the controller:
def update
  @user.avatar.attach(params[:avatar])
end
directAnswer: Active Storage attaches files to models and supports local or cloud-backed storage, direct uploads, metadata and image variants.
explanation: Authorize uploads/downloads, impose size and content-type policies, and do not rely only on a supplied filename or browser MIME type. Isolate uploaded content and process expensive image/video work asynchronously. Direct uploads reduce web-server bandwidth but still require access controls, lifecycle cleanup and malware/content checks appropriate to the application.
example:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_one_attached :avatar
end
user.avatar.attach(io: File.open("avatar.png"), filename: "avatar.png", content_type: "image/png")

question: What is ActiveRecord::Enum in Rails?
sourceAnswer:
ActiveRecord::Enum provides a way to map an integer column to a set of symbolic values, allowing you to use human-readable symbols instead of raw integers in your code. This simplifies working with enumerated types and improves code readability. For example:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  enum role: { guest: 0, user: 1, admin: 2 }
end
The enum method maps the role column to three symbolic values: guest, user, and admin.
directAnswer: Rails enum maps an attribute to named states backed by explicit integer or string values.
explanation: Use explicit mappings so adding or reordering names does not reinterpret existing database values. Modern Rails uses positional name/value arguments. Ruby itself has no general enum keyword corresponding to this Rails macro.

question: Describe how to implement a Rails callback for setting a default value before creating a record.
sourceAnswer:
Rails callbacks like before_create allow you to execute code before a record is saved to the database. You can use this callback to set default values for attributes before the record is created. For example:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  before_create :set_default_status

  private

  def set_default_status
    self.status ||= 'active'
  end
end
The before_create callback invokes set_default_status before the user record is created, setting the status attribute to 'active' if it is not already set.
directAnswer: Model callbacks hook into persistence lifecycle events; controller callbacks run before, after or around actions. Keep their responsibilities explicit.
explanation: Use before_validation to normalize values before validation and before_save/before_create for appropriate persistence preparation. after_save still runs within the transaction; prefer after_commit or an outbox for external side effects. An around_action must yield to run the action. after_action is not an ensure block and is not guaranteed after exceptions. Controller rendering/redirecting from a before action can halt the callback chain.
example:
before_validation :normalize_name
private
def normalize_name
  self.name = name.to_s.strip
end
# External side effect after persistence:
# after_commit :enqueue_notification, on: :create

question: Explain how Rails handles logging.
sourceAnswer:
Rails uses ActiveSupport::Logger to manage logging, which records events, errors, and information to files in the log directory. It supports various log levels like DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL, allowing developers to track different types of messages.

Logging settings can be adjusted in environment configuration files, enabling control over log verbosity and output locations. This setup helps in monitoring and debugging by providing a structured way to capture and view application logs.
directAnswer: Use structured request/error context, logs, traces, metrics and focused debugging to identify the failing operation, then add a regression check.
explanation: Log to the configured destination, often stdout in containers or log/<environment>.log locally. Filter secrets and personal data. Track latency, error rate, queue age, database saturation and resource usage. Use the debug gem or a local console for interactive inspection; do not expose development error consoles publicly. Apache logs live wherever the web server is configured, not at a universal Rails path.
example:
Rails.logger.info(event: "order_created", order_id: order.id, request_id: request.request_id)

question: How does Rails support internationalization (i18n) and what is an example of using locale files for translations?
sourceAnswer:
Rails supports internationalization (i18n) through locale files that contain translations for different languages. These files are stored in the config/locales directory and are used to provide multilingual support for your application. For example:

en:
  hello: "Hello"
The locale file en.yml defines a translation for the hello key in English.
directAnswer: Rails uses the I18n library and locale data to translate messages and localize dates, numbers and other presentation.
explanation: Keep translations in config/locales, use t/l helpers, and select a permitted locale per request with I18n.with_locale so it does not leak between requests. Handle pluralization and missing translations, and keep timezone selection separate from language selection.
example:

en:
  hello: "Hello"
# Ruby:

question: Discuss the Rails delegate method.
sourceAnswer:
The delegate method in Rails is used to delegate method calls to an associated object, simplifying your code and reducing the need for redundant code. This is useful when you want to expose methods of an associated object directly from the parent model. For example:

class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_one :profile
  delegate :full_name, to: :profile
end

class Profile < ApplicationRecord
  def full_name
    "#{first_name} #{last_name}"
  end
end
The delegate method in the User model allows you to call user.full_name directly, which delegates the method call to the profile association. This simplifies accessing the full_name method from the Profile model.
directAnswer: delegate forwards selected methods to a named object, reducing repetitive forwarding code.
explanation: This exposes a smaller interface without inheritance. Choose prefix: when forwarding could clash with local methods, and allow_nil: only if missing targets should return nil. Delegation does not automatically remove all domain or framework coupling.
example:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_one :profile
  delegate :full_name, to: :profile, prefix: true, allow_nil: true
end
user.profile_full_name

question: How does Rails handle polymorphic associations?
sourceAnswer:
Polymorphic associations allow a model to belong to more than one other model using a single association. This is achieved by using type and ID columns to refer to the associated model. For example:

class Comment < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :commentable, polymorphic: true
end

class Post < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :comments, as: :commentable
end

class Event < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :comments, as: :commentable
end
The Comment model can be associated with both Post and Event models using a single commentable association.
directAnswer: A polymorphic belongs_to stores both the associated record’s ID and its model type so one association can point to different model classes.
explanation: The owner side declares has_many or has_one with as:, and the child declares belongs_to with polymorphic: true. The child belongs to one owner at a time, rather than simultaneously belonging to every model type. A conventional single foreign key cannot enforce references to multiple owner tables, so consider data integrity and class renames carefully.
example:
class Comment < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :commentable, polymorphic: true
end
class Post < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :comments, as: :commentable
end
# Columns: commentable_id and commentable_type

question: What is Ruby on Rails, and what are its main features?
sourceAnswer:
Ruby on Rails, commonly known as Rails, is a full-stack web application framework built using the Ruby programming language. It was created by David Heinemeier Hansson in 2004 to streamline the web development process by emphasizing developer productivity and ease of use. Rails follows the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architectural pattern, which separates the application into three primary components, allowing for better code organization, maintainability, and scalability.

Main Features of Ruby on Rails:

MVC Architecture: The Model-View-Controller (MVC) design pattern is the core of Rails. It organizes code into three parts:some text
Model: Represents the data and business logic of the application.
View: Represents the user interface and is responsible for displaying data to the user.
Controller: Manages the flow of data between models and views, responding to user requests.
Convention over Configuration: Rails emphasizes convention over configuration, which means that it assumes sensible defaults (e.g., table names, file structures) so developers don't have to explicitly configure them, making it easier and faster to get started with development.
ActiveRecord ORM: ActiveRecord is Rails' built-in Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) layer. It abstracts the interaction with the database, allowing developers to work with database records as Ruby objects, rather than writing raw SQL queries.
RESTful Routing: Rails encourages using REST (Representational State Transfer) for organizing routes and managing resources. This makes it easier to follow predictable, maintainable routes for actions like creating, reading, updating, and deleting records.
Scaffolding: Rails allows you to generate default code (models, controllers, views) for basic CRUD operations using scaffolding commands. This dramatically speeds up development.
Asset Pipeline: The Rails asset pipeline helps manage JavaScript, CSS, and image files, providing features like minification, concatenation, and compilation (e.g., CoffeeScript to JavaScript, Sass to CSS).
Built-in Testing Framework: Rails comes with a robust testing framework, encouraging Test-Driven Development (TDD) and ensuring high-quality, bug-free applications.
Security Features: Rails includes built-in security features like Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) protection, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection, and SQL Injection prevention.
Tooling and Gems: Rails offers a rich ecosystem of libraries (called gems) that extend the functionality of your application, such as authentication, authorization, background job processing, and more.
directAnswer: Rails is an open-source web application framework written in Ruby, organized around MVC, convention over configuration, and avoiding duplicated knowledge.
explanation: Its integrated routing, Active Record, templates, migrations, jobs and testing support reduce routine application setup. Conventions provide useful defaults, while configuration allows exceptions. Rails can be used for HTML applications or JSON APIs. question: What are Models, Views, and Controllers in Rails?
sourceAnswer:
In Ruby on Rails, Models, Views, and Controllers (MVC) are the core components of the framework. The MVC architecture helps separate the application’s logic, presentation, and data management, which improves maintainability and scalability. Model: The Model represents the application’s data and business logic. It interacts with the database, validating, saving, and retrieving data. Models typically correspond to tables in the database and are responsible for defining relationships between different models (e.g., has_many, belongs_to). ‍ Example: class User < ApplicationRecord validates :name, presence: true has_many :posts end View: The View represents the user interface. It renders the data passed by the controller into a readable format (usually HTML), often mixed with Ruby code. Views are where developers define the structure of web pages that users will see. Example (in ERB template format):erb

Welcome, <%= @user.name %>!

Controller: The Controller serves as the bridge between the Model and the View. It processes user requests, interacts with the model to retrieve or manipulate data, and then decides which view to render. Controllers contain actions that are triggered by specific routes and HTTP methods. Example: ruby class UsersController < ApplicationController def show @user = User.find(params[:id]) end end using associations such as has_many, belongs_to, has_one, and has_and_belongs_to_many. Example: ruby class Post < ApplicationRecord belongs_to :user has_many :comments end Validations: Active Record allows you to validate data before it is saved to the database, ensuring that it meets specific criteria (e.g., presence, uniqueness, numerically). Example: ruby class User < ApplicationRecord validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true end Active Record enables developers to work with data using object-oriented principles, which increases productivity and reduces the amount of boilerplate SQL code.
directAnswer: MVC separates domain/data behavior in models, presentation in views, and request coordination in controllers.
explanation: The router dispatches a request to a controller action. The action loads or changes domain objects and renders a view or another representation, or returns a redirect. Active Record models often provide persistence, but a model need not inherit from Active Record. Views should avoid database queries, and complex workflows can live in services or other domain objects.
example:
# app/controllers/posts_controller.rb def show @post = Post.find(params[:id]) end # app/views/posts/show.html.erb

<%= @post.title %>

question: Explain the concept of RESTful routes in Rails.
sourceAnswer:
RESTful routing is an architectural pattern that defines how web applications should handle HTTP requests. Rails encourages the use of REST (Representational State Transfer) to manage the CRUD operations for resources in a consistent and predictable manner.

In Rails, a resource refers to an entity that your application manages (e.g., a User, Post, or Comment). Rails generates routes for these resources using the resources keyword.

RESTful Routes:

For a resource like posts, the following routes are automatically created:

GET /posts: Index action (lists all posts).
GET /posts/:id: Show action (displays a single post).
POST /posts: Create action (creates a new post).
PATCH/PUT /posts/:id: Update action (modifies an existing post).
DELETE /posts/:id: Destroy action (deletes a post).
These routes map to specific actions in the controller (e.g., index, show, create, update, destroy), making it easier to organize the application and follow a standardized approach to handling data.

The new/edit routes display forms; they do not themselves persist changes. A member route has an ID and a collection route does not. Match action names exactly.

question: What are migrations in Rails, and why are they important?
sourceAnswer:
Migrations in Rails are a way to manage changes to the database schema over time. They allow you to modify the database structure without writing raw SQL, making schema changes easy to version-control and apply consistently across different environments.

Why Migrations Are Important:

Version Control: Migrations allow you to track changes to the database schema, making it easier to collaborate with others and deploy schema changes in a controlled manner.
Reversibility: Migrations are reversible, meaning you can undo changes if necessary, using the rails db:rollback command.
Consistency: Migrations ensure that database changes are applied consistently across different development, staging, and production environments.
Example of a Migration:

To generate a migration to add a new column to the user's table:

bash

rails generate migration AddAgeToUsers age:integer

‍

To apply the migration and update the schema:

bash

rails db:migrate

‍
directAnswer: Migrations are versioned Ruby schema changes; run bin/rails db:migrate to apply them and bin/rails db:rollback to undo the latest reversible migration.
explanation: Use change for reversible operations, or up/down/reversible when Rails cannot infer reversal. Rails records applied migration versions in schema_migrations and maintains schema.rb or structure.sql. Do not edit already-applied migrations to change production schema. Adapter-specific SQL and some DDL cannot be portable or reversible, and rollback may lose data.
example:
bin/rails generate migration AddAgeToUsers age:integer
# Generated class version matches the app:
def change
  add_column :users, :age, :integer
end
bin/rails db:migrate
importantPoints: ruby script/generate and class-level self.up/self.down examples are legacy syntax; modern migrations normally use versioned classes and instance methods.

question: What is the difference between render and redirect_to in controllers?
sourceAnswer:
Both render and redirect_to are methods used in Rails controllers, but they have different purposes and behaviors:

render: The render method is used to render a specific view template, either the default view for the current action or a different one. When you call render, the controller action will continue processing and the same request will be reused, meaning the browser's URL won't change. Example: ruby :ruby

def show
  @post = Post.find(params[:id])
  render :show  # Renders the show.html.erb view
end
redirect_to: The redirect to method is used to send an HTTP response that tells the browser to make a new request to a different URL. This causes the browser's URL to change, and the corresponding action and view are processed. ExampleExample ruby

def create
  @post = Post.new(post_params)
  if @post.save
    redirect_to @post  # Redirects the user to the show page of the newly created post
  else
    render :new  # Renders the new.html.erb view in case of failure
  end
end
Key Difference:

render keeps the URL the same and just renders a view.
redirect_to changes the URL and sends a new request to the browser.
directAnswer: render builds the response within the current request; redirect_to returns an HTTP redirect so the client makes another request.
explanation: Rendering another template does not run that template’s controller action, so initialize its required data. Neither render nor redirect_to is a Ruby control-flow return; use return or conditional structure to avoid unintended continuation or double rendering. Use an appropriate failure status for invalid submissions.
example:
if @post.save
  redirect_to @post, status: :see_other
else
  render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity
end

question: What is a partial in Rails, and why would you use it?
